youtube.title: 5 mistakes killing your padel defense
titleOptions: How to defend off the glass in padel
Stop losing points in padel defense
youtube.description: Struggling to defend off the glass in padel? Here are the 5 biggest mistakes amateur players make on defense — and the exact court science to turn wall balls into counter-attacks.

scenes.narration: Imagine standing at the back of a padel court, pinned against the glass while two opponents smash volleys at your feet.
Every ball feels like a blur, your racket clips the wall, and the point ends before you can react.
Today, I will show you the 5 mistakes destroying your defense, and the court science to turn every wall ball into an attack.

scenes.label: of points won by the team at the net
scenes.narration: In padel, over 80 percent of points are won by the team controlling the net.
Defending is not about surviving indefinitely at the baseline.
Defense has one goal: neutralize the attack, evict opponents from the net, and take it back.

scenes.title: Racket sport habits in padel
scenes.narration: Most players fail because they bring habits from tennis, squash, or pickleball into an enclosed glass court.

scenes.title: The 5 defensive traps
scenes.narration: Here are the 5 traps keeping you locked at the back.

scenes.heading: Late corner turns
scenes.narration: The hardest place to defend in padel is the 90-degree corner between the rear and side glass.
When a ball enters this corner, it hits both walls, creating a double glass rebound.
The fatal mistake is running straight into the corner facing the glass, waiting for the ball to hit both walls before turning.
By then, the ball bounces off the second wall directly into your hip, pinning you with zero room.
Trying to pivot on high-traction turf with your foot planted twists your knee, creating dangerous rotational shear on your meniscus.
To fix this, read which glass the ball strikes first.
If the ball hits the side wall first, that is an opening double.
Open the door immediately: take a mini split-step, pivot your hips 180 degrees with flexed knees, and maintain 1 meter of clearance from the glass.
Think of a revolving door: turn with the curve, never fight against it.
If the ball hits the back wall first, that is a closing double.
Do not spin in circles here.
Keep your chest facing the side wall, take two small steps forward, and catch the rebound as it leaves the back glass.

scenes.title: Open-The-Door Drill
scenes.narration: Train this with the Open-the-Door drill: start with gentle feeds for 4 sets of 10 side-first corner balls before adding match pace.
Pivot on the balls of your feet with soft knees before glass contact, guiding the rebound smoothly down the line.

scenes.heading: Hugging the back glass
scenes.narration: When heavy smashes rain down from the net, your natural instinct is to back up until your heels touch the back glass.
This is called the safety illusion.
You think standing farther away gives you more time, but hugging the glass destroys your defense.
First, you have zero backswing room, so your paddle smacks the glass and you push weak balls forward.

scenes.label: incoming speed rebounded by tempered glass
scenes.narration: Second, tempered glass rebounds about 70 percent of incoming speed, launching deep shots 1 to 2 meters into the court.
If you are standing against the wall, the ball rebounds behind your body.

scenes.label: unprotected desert between baseline and net
scenes.narration: Third, standing against the wall creates a massive 7-meter empty desert between you and the net, giving opponents easy drop shots.
The fix is anchoring yourself in the defensive sweet spot: 0.8 meters behind the service line, and 1 meter in from the side glass.
Standing here is like a soccer goalkeeper positioning off the goal line.
When a short ball comes, step forward across the line.
When a deep ball comes, track backward with crossover steps, keeping a 1-meter deceleration buffer from the back wall.
Strike it at waist height as it rebounds forward into the court.

scenes.title: Service-Line Tether Drill
scenes.narration: Train this with the Service-Line Tether drill: mark your sweet spot with cones 0.8 meters behind the service line.
Have a feeder alternate between a short ball and a deep glass ball for 4 sets of 8 cycles.
Strike the short ball, and glide backward using controlled crossover steps to touch your cone.
Track both ball and wall, letting the glass feed the rebound right into your strike zone.

scenes.heading: Blasting flat counter-punches
scenes.narration: When players are pinned deep under heavy pressure, they panic and blast a flat, 60-mile-per-hour missile straight at net players.
This is the single most self-destructive shot in padel.
At 7 meters away, net players hold solid composite rackets with no strings.
A hard flat shot hits their racket and rebounds with devastating pace, giving them an instant reflex winner.

scenes.label: increase in unforced errors from baseline speed-ups
scenes.narration: Attempting flat speed-ups from deep court increases your unforced errors by over 4-fold.
Firing hard at net players is like throwing rocks at a tank: you only give them the ammunition to crush you.
The true weapon of padel defense is the high reset lob.

scenes.title: Defensive transition efficacy
scenes.narration: In professional padel, players choose the lob in over 60 percent of defensive transitions, keeping the rally alive and neutralizing the attack nearly two-thirds of the time.

scenes.label: hang time created by a 5 to 8 meter lob
scenes.narration: A proper defensive lob arches 5 to 8 meters into the air, creating 3.5 to 4.5 seconds of flight hang time.
Those 4 seconds break opponents' rhythm, force both volleyers to sprint 7 meters backward, and give you time to capture the net.
To hit it, bend your knees, open your paddle face 25 degrees, and lift smoothly from your legs without snapping your wrist.

scenes.title: Stopwatch Lob Drill
scenes.narration: Practice the Stopwatch Lob drill: hit lobs from the baseline with a partner timing the ball in the air.
Do 4 sets of 10 repetitions, counting only lobs that hang for at least 3.5 seconds and land in the back third.

scenes.heading: Forgetting the chiquita
scenes.narration: Sometimes opponents anticipate your lob, standing 3 to 4 meters back from the net with overheads cocked.
Or you play in an indoor club with a low ceiling where sky-high lobs are restricted.
When amateurs cannot lob, they usually hit a medium-pace drive right at the opponent's chest.
This lets net players lean forward and punch an aggressive angle off the side fence.
The secret weapon here is the chiquita, which means "the little one."
A chiquita is a slow, dipping slice that crosses inches over the net and dies right at your opponent's shoelaces.

scenes.label: center net height threshold in padel
scenes.narration: Padel net height is 0.88 meters at the center.
If opponents contact the ball above the net, they can spike downward into the glass.
When your chiquita dips below net height, physics forces them to volley upward just to clear the tape.
The instant they hit that floating upward ball, your defense flips into an attack.
To execute it, cushion the ball with a compact slice backswing, applying gentle backspin so it dips immediately.
Most importantly, only advance once the ball visibly dips below net tape height.
Take two quick steps forward into the transition zone, split-step with paddle chest-high, and pounce on their floating volley.

scenes.title: Shoelace Drop Drill
scenes.narration: Train this with the Shoelace Drop drill: place target hoops 1.5 meters behind the net.
Feed balls from the baseline, alternating between high reset lobs and soft dipping chiquitas, aiming for 4 sets of 12 reps.

scenes.heading: The center ball freeze
scenes.narration: The padel court is 10 meters wide, and opponents love driving the ball straight down the center seam between partners.
Amateur pairs either both freeze, letting the ball roll off the glass, or both swing, clashing rackets and risking hand injuries.

scenes.label: open canyon down the middle when partner freezes
scenes.narration: Even worse, when one player gets pulled wide into a corner, the other stands still, leaving a 4-meter canyon down the middle.
Spatial tracking shows that elite pairs move as a synchronized unit, connected by an invisible 3-meter string.
When your partner slides wide to the right corner, you must slide right to seal the center seam.
Next, establish middle priority before the point begins.
The default rule is forehand in the middle: for two right-handed players, the left-side player takes contested center balls because their forehand has natural leverage.
If you are playing cross-court, the player diagonally opposite the hitter covers the drive.

scenes.sub: Shout while ball is in the air
scenes.narration: Above all, enforce the early call-or-yield rule: the moment the ball crosses the net tape, shout "Mine."
If no call is heard, the secondary partner must immediately yield and clear the hitting corridor.
Calling early eliminates hesitation and lets your partner step aside to cover the next angle.

scenes.title: Center Calling Drill
scenes.narration: Practice the Center Calling drill: have a feeder fire rapid groundstrokes down the center line for 4 sets of 12 balls.
Call "Mine" while the ball is airborne over the net, scoop a defensive lob, and coordinate seamless coverage without a single collision.

scenes.heading: The defensive blueprint
scenes.narration: To lock these 5 fixes into your muscle memory, follow this simple weekly court plan.

scenes.title: Session 1: Corner Reads
scenes.narration: In session one, spend 15 minutes on corner glass reads: 4 sets of 10 reps of the Open-the-Door drill, alternating side-first and back-first rebounds.

scenes.title: Session 2: Transition Mastery
scenes.narration: In session two, dedicate 15 minutes to transition mastery: 4 sets of 10 Stopwatch Lobs and 4 sets of 8 Chiquita-and-Pounce sequences.
During match play, make the sweet spot your home base: 0.8 meters behind the service line, connected to your partner by that invisible string.

scenes.title: 8-Minute Warm-Up Routine
scenes.narration: Always complete an 8-minute warm-up with dynamic ankle calf lunges, lateral hip openers, and standing thoracic spine rotations with your racket across your shoulders.
If you feel sudden knee locking, sharp wrist shock after contact, or cannot bear weight on your ankle, stop immediately and see a sports physiotherapist or sports medicine physician.

scenes.sub: Turn defense into your greatest weapon
scenes.narration: Padel defense is not about panic, scrambling, or hitting harder.
Master the geometry of the glass, command the defensive sweet spot, and let the walls become your greatest ally. See you on the court.
